text.content:
You wake with the taste of metal on your tongue.

For a moment, you do not know what has disturbed you. You lie beneath the heavy woollen blankets, caught between sleep and waking, listening to a sound that seems to come from everywhere at once. It is low and continuous, a deep, unnatural hum that vibrates through the bedframe and into your bones. The wooden boards beneath you tremble. Somewhere above, the rafters creak with the strained complaint of a ship caught in a storm.

Then you smell the smoke.

It is not the familiar scent of woodsmoke that clings to the cottage walls, nor the comforting trace of last night's fire. This is sharper, bitter and metallic, like iron left too long in rainwater. It catches at the back of your throat and makes your eyes sting. A thin veil of violet-grey smoke seeps through the gaps between the floorboards, curling around the legs of the bed before spreading across the room.

You drag in a breath and immediately regret it.

The smoke tastes of ash and something sour, something that seems to settle on your tongue rather than enter your lungs. You cough, twisting the blankets away from your face. The air is thick enough to make breathing feel like work, and every breath brings that strange metallic flavour back.

Outside, someone screams.

The sound tears through the night, followed by a crash so violent that your cottage shudders around you. Glass breaks somewhere nearby, not in a single sharp burst but in a long, rippling series of cracks. The noise carries an impossible quality, as though an enormous sheet of glass is being bent beyond its limits, every fracture spreading into the next. Beneath it all, the hum grows louder.

You sit upright.

The room is wrong.

Moonlight should fall through the small window above your table, silvering the edge of the washbasin and catching the familiar shapes of your furniture. Instead, violet light crawls across the walls. It shifts and twists without any visible source, stretching the shadows of the chair and table into long, distorted shapes. The dark corners seem to breathe. Every few moments, the light pulses, and the cottage responds with another faint shudder.

You press your palm against the mattress to steady yourself.

The vibration is not simply something you hear. You feel it in your teeth, in the hollow of your chest, in the joints of your fingers. It runs through the bedstead and into the floor, a rapid, delicate trembling that makes your skin tighten. Your heartbeat seems to fall out of rhythm with it. For one disorienting instant, you cannot tell whether the shaking comes from the cottage or from inside your own body.

Then the roof groans.

A shower of dust drifts from the ceiling. One of the rafters gives a sharp crack, and something heavy shifts overhead. You stare up, scarcely breathing, as the sound travels from one end of the cottage to the other.

Whatever is happening outside, it is not confined to the village green.

It is here.

It is beneath your feet, in the walls, in the air you are struggling to breathe.

You throw the blankets aside and swing your legs over the edge of the bed. The floor is cold beneath your bare feet. When you stand, the room tilts slightly, and you reach for the bedpost until the dizziness passes. Smoke drifts around your ankles. Through the window, you can see flashes of violet light moving between the houses, bright enough to cast the crooked silhouettes of chimneys and rooflines across the clouds.

There are more screams now.

A man's voice calls for someone. A child cries out, the sound abruptly swallowed by another terrible crash. Somewhere beyond the cottage, an animal bellows in panic. You hear hurried footsteps on the lane, followed by a thud and a cry of pain.

The village you knew yesterday has become a place of confusion and terror in the space between one breath and the next.

Your first thought is not of the forest, nor of the strange occurrences that troubled the evening. It is of the people who may be in danger. Of the doors that need opening, the paths that may already be blocked, and the precious seconds that disappear while you stand in the dark trying to understand.

But fear takes different shapes in different people.

Your heart hammers against your ribs, and the sound seems impossibly loud beneath the humming air. You do not stop to decide whether the danger is real. The thought of someone being trapped in the smoke, unable to find their way through the darkness, is enough to drive you into motion.

You shout down the hallway.

Names come before questions. You call for your family, your voice roughened by smoke, refusing to be silenced by the strange vibration in the walls. You need to hear an answer. You need to know that the people you love are awake, that they understand something terrible is happening, that you have not been left alone in this nightmare.

When the roof cracks again, you barely flinch. Your attention is fixed on the rooms beyond your bedroom, on the possibility of a familiar voice answering you through the smoke.

You will not leave without knowing who is safe.

Not if you can help it.

Panic arrives as a cold pressure in your chest, but you push it aside before it can take hold. Whatever this is, the cottage is becoming dangerous. The smoke is gathering close to the floor, the roof is under strain, and the strange vibration is making it difficult to judge what might collapse next.

You lower yourself instinctively, keeping your head beneath the thickest of the smoke. The air near the floor seems marginally clearer. You take one shallow breath through your sleeve and begin to assess the room.

The door is several steps away. The hallway beyond it may offer a route to the back entrance, but you cannot know whether the passage is clear. The front door opens onto the lane, where the noise suggests debris, fire, or something worse. The windows are narrow, and the one beside your bed is too small to make an easy escape.

You force yourself to notice details rather than imagine disasters. The direction of the smoke. The angle of the nearest rafter. The position of your boots. The location of the household's spare lantern.

Your hands tremble as you reach for your clothes, but you do not let that stop you.

There will be time to be afraid when you are somewhere safer.

You make no sound.

You sit motionless on the edge of the bed, watching violet shadows writhe across the walls. The smoke creeps around your feet, and the vibration travels through your bones with such strange insistence that you feel, for a moment, as though the cottage itself has become a living thing.

You do not call out. You do not cry for help. You listen.

A scream from the lane. The crash of breaking glass. A frantic pounding somewhere nearby, followed by silence. Each sound becomes a point on an invisible map, marking the places where the night is coming apart.

Your gaze moves from the window to the door, then to the narrow hallway beyond. You measure the distance between them without consciously deciding to do so. You note the shifting shadows beneath the door and the way the smoke thickens whenever the vibration rises.

Fear is there, but it has driven you inward rather than outward. You feel it in the cold sweat gathering beneath your nightclothes, in the tightness of your jaw, in the effort it takes to make your fingers move.

You cannot understand what is happening.

You can, however, observe it.

And you have the unsettling feeling that whatever has entered the village may already know you are awake.

A fresh tremor rolls through the cottage. The table scrapes across the floor with a harsh, wooden groan. Something falls from the shelf beside the hearth and shatters. The violet light flares, illuminating the smoke until the entire room seems filled with suspended ash.

You turn towards the rest of your household.

Your parents are in the adjacent room.

You hear them before you see them: a violent bout of coughing, followed by the scrape of furniture being dragged across the floor. Your mother calls your name, but the words dissolve into another fit of choking. Your father's voice follows, strained and furious, as though he is trying to force the world back into order by sheer stubbornness.

You rush towards their door.

The hallway is choked with smoke, and the air grows hotter as you approach the adjoining room. A timber lintel has fallen across the doorway, its splintered end wedged against the frame. Beyond it, you can make out your parents' shapes through the shifting haze. Your mother is bent over, one hand braced against the wall. Your father is trying to move a fallen beam, but it shifts only a fraction before settling back into place.

The sight sends a sharp, helpless pain through you.

They are alive. They are trapped. And the cottage is beginning to come apart around them.

Another crack runs through the ceiling. Dust rains down over your shoulders. The timber blocking the doorway groans as the structure above it shifts, and you realise that whatever you do, you cannot afford to waste time.

Isleen is huddled beside your bed.

You had not noticed them in the darkness. They sit pressed against the wall, knees drawn tightly to their chest, their face pale beneath the violet light. Their eyes are fixed on you, wide and glassy with terror. They must have woken before you, or perhaps they came to your room when the screaming began. Either way, they have been sitting here alone while the world outside collapsed into noise.

When they reach for you, their fingers are so cold that you feel it through your skin.

They try to speak, but no words come. Their mouth opens and closes, and their gaze darts towards the window each time another crash shakes the cottage. They are too frightened to stand. Every instinct seems to have deserted them, leaving only the desperate need to remain close to something familiar.

You kneel beside them. The smoke catches in your throat, and the floor shivers beneath your knees.

Your sibling clutches your arm.

You can feel them trembling.

Beyond the bedroom door, something heavy scrapes across the hallway floor. The roof groans again, louder this time, and a thin crack appears in the plaster above the window.

You cannot remain here for long. But you cannot simply run, either.

Whatever happens next, your sibling will have to come with you.

There is no answering voice from another room.

No footsteps approach your door. No familiar hand reaches for yours. No one calls your name through the smoke.

You are alone in the cottage.

The knowledge should make the decision easier. There is no one to find, no one to carry, no one whose safety must be weighed against your own. You can leave as soon as you find a way out.

Yet the room feels more threatening than it did a moment ago.

The violet light gathers in the corners, pulsing faintly against the stone walls. The vibration seems to change whenever you move. When you take a step towards the door, it rises into a thin, painful tremor that runs through your teeth. When you stop, it settles into a low hum that you feel more than hear.

A bead of cold sweat slides down your spine.

You turn towards the window. Outside, the lane is filled with smoke, and something moves beyond the opposite cottage. You cannot tell whether it is a person stumbling through the haze or a shadow cast by the unnatural light.

Then the air around you tightens.

For one terrible instant, you feel a pressure against your skin, as though an unseen hand has closed around the cottage and is testing the strength of its walls. The sensation is so intimate, so deliberate, that your breath catches.

The vibration deepens.

You have no proof that whatever is happening has noticed you. No reason to believe the strange pressure is anything more than the effects of smoke, fear, and a building on the verge of collapse.

But your skin prickles with cold sweat, and you cannot shake the conviction that the danger in the room is not entirely outside it.

You stagger back as another impact shakes the cottage. Above you, timber splits with a sound like a tree breaking under winter ice. A crack races across the ceiling, branching through the plaster. For a moment, the entire room is illuminated by a violet flash, bright enough to turn every familiar object into a stark, colourless shape.

Then darkness returns, broken only by the shifting glow outside.

You understand, finally, that this is not a night you can wait out beneath your blankets. The cottage that has sheltered you for years may not survive the next few minutes. The smoke is thickening, the roof is failing, and the air itself seems charged with a force you cannot name.

You have only moments to decide what matters most.

The door is within reach. The window offers another possible escape. Beyond the walls, people are screaming, and the village is filling with violet-grey smoke. Somewhere in the chaos there may be a way to safety, but you cannot see it from here.

The floor trembles once more beneath your feet.

What is your immediate priority as the roof begins to crack?

choices.text: Focus entirely on getting your family (or yourself) out to safety, ignoring the village square completely
Risk everything to grab your family heirlooms and hidden papers before running into the chaos.
Rush straight out the front door to confront whatever is burning your home.

text.content:
You make the decision before you have fully understood what is happening.

The screams from the village square are too terrible, the violet light too unnatural. Whatever has descended upon the settlement, you know with sudden certainty that you cannot fight it. You cannot help everyone. You cannot even begin to understand what you are facing.

But you may still be able to save the people closest to you.

You turn away from the front door.

The decision feels like tearing something loose inside yourself. Every instinct urges you towards the noise, towards the voices calling for help and the homes that have sheltered your neighbours for generations. You know the village. You know its people. You have shared their bread, their work, their celebrations, and their grief. Somewhere beyond the smoke, someone you have known all your life may be trapped beneath a fallen beam or stumbling through the dark in search of a loved one.

You force yourself not to think about it.

The roof groans overhead. Dust falls across your shoulders, and another violent shudder runs through the cottage. You move towards the back of the house, keeping low beneath the smoke. The violet-grey haze has begun to seep through the walls and around the window frames, carrying that same bitter, metallic taste. Your eyes water. Each breath scrapes at your throat.

You reach the rear shutters and wrench them open.

Cold night air rushes into the room, bringing with it the smell of damp grass, turned earth, and something burning far more fiercely than wood. Beyond the window lies the little orchard behind your cottage. The trees stand in uneven rows, their bare branches black against the strange illumination spreading across the sky. Fallen leaves cling to the wet ground. Beyond them, the land slopes towards the dark boundary of the woods.

It is not a good escape route. The orchard is uneven, the ground slick with rain, and the trees offer little protection if whatever is happening reaches this far.

It is, however, a way out.

You turn towards your household.

Your parents are coughing in the adjoining room, and the sound sharpens your fear into something almost unbearable. The fallen timber blocking their doorway has already begun to shift under the strain of the collapsing roof.

You cannot leave them behind.

You hurry back, dragging at the broken beam until it scrapes aside far enough for them to squeeze through. Your father protests that he can manage on his own, even as he struggles to draw breath. Your mother grips your arm with such force that her fingers hurt. Neither of them asks where you intend to go. They have heard the screams. They have felt the house tremble. They know that whatever comes next, staying here is no longer an option.

You help them towards the rear window, supporting your mother when her footing falters and urging your father to keep moving. The three of you make it outside just as another crack splits the roof.

Isleen is still huddled beside the bed, shaking so badly that they struggle to stand. When you reach for them, they seize your hand and refuse to let go.

You do not waste time trying to explain what is happening. There are no words that could make sense of the violet light or the impossible noise outside. You tell them that you are leaving, that they must stay close, and that they must do exactly as you say.

They nod, though their eyes remain fixed on the window.

You wrap a blanket around their shoulders and guide them towards the open shutters. They hesitate at the drop to the ground, looking back towards the familiar room, but you climb out first and reach up for them. When their feet finally touch the wet grass, they cling to you as another tremendous crash shakes the cottage.

You hold them close for one brief moment.

Then you turn towards the orchard.

There is no one else to rescue from the cottage.

For one brief moment, you stand in the middle of the room, listening to the destruction outside. You could go towards the village square. You could try to find the source of the violet light, or help the people whose screams still carry through the night.

But you have no weapon, no understanding of the force tearing through the settlement, and no reason to believe that approaching it would accomplish anything except getting you killed.

You choose the orchard.

You gather your cloak and whatever you can carry without slowing yourself down. The practical familiarity of these movements feels almost obscene against the chaos outside. You are preparing to leave your home as though you were setting out on an ordinary journey, checking your belongings and fastening your clothes while the world tears itself apart.

Then the roof cracks above you.

You climb through the shutters and drop into the wet grass.

You do not look back.

The orchard is almost completely dark beneath the violet glow. You move between the trees, slipping on wet leaves and stumbling over exposed roots. The smoke follows you, gathering in the hollows between the trunks, but the air grows clearer as you move away from the cottage. Behind you, the village has become a shifting landscape of unnatural colour and black silhouettes.

You reach the far edge of the orchard just as your cottage collapses.

The sound is enormous. Timber splinters, slate tiles tumble, and the walls give way with a roar that seems to shake the earth beneath your feet. A cloud of sparks bursts upwards, briefly illuminating the orchard in violent shades of violet and white. You flinch and turn your face away as fragments of burning debris scatter across the garden.

For a moment, you can see the place where you have lived for years.

The window through which you watched the evening settle. The doorway you crossed a thousand times. The roof beneath which you slept, ate, argued, laughed, and made plans for mornings that now seem impossibly distant.

Then smoke swallows it.

You keep moving.

The trees grow closer together as you leave the orchard behind. Branches catch at your clothes, and brambles scrape your hands. The ground slopes into a shallow hollow before rising towards the forest boundary. You know these woods well enough to avoid the worst of the uneven ground, but tonight familiar paths offer little comfort. The trees seem taller than you remember, their trunks disappearing into a darkness that the violet light cannot quite penetrate.

You do not stop until the village is hidden behind the ridge.

There, beneath the shelter of the trees, you find a place where the ground rises above a narrow stream. You settle into the freezing mud and draw your household close, or crouch alone beneath the branches, depending on who has survived the journey with you. Your clothes are damp. Your hands ache from the cold. Every distant crash makes you tense, and every sudden silence feels worse than the noise that preceded it.

From the ridge, you watch your home burn.

The violet fires do not behave like ordinary flames. They climb walls without consuming them, then devour entire rooftops in moments. They flare in strange, angular patterns, bending against the wind as though following invisible currents. At times, the light grows so bright that the village appears carved from glass. Then whole streets disappear into darkness, leaving only a few scattered points of colour among the smoke.

You see no people clearly enough to recognise them.

Occasionally, a figure moves between the burning houses, but the distance and the shifting haze make it impossible to tell whether they are villagers fleeing the destruction or something else entirely. You hear the distant hum even here, though the trees soften its edges. It travels through the ground and into your bones, a persistent vibration that makes the earth beneath you feel strangely alive.

Hours pass.

The cold settles into your clothes. Your legs grow stiff, and your mouth is dry from the smoke. If you have brought your family, you do what you can to keep them warm, sharing your cloak and murmuring whatever words might persuade them to remain quiet. If you are alone, you have only your own breathing to listen to, and the distant sounds of a village being unmade.

Eventually, the violet fires begin to fade.

Their brightness diminishes first, shrinking from towering sheets of colour to isolated flickers. The unnatural hum weakens. One by one, the burning houses fall dark, leaving behind a grey, lifeless smoulder. Smoke drifts over the rooftops, and the first hint of dawn begins to pale the eastern sky.

You might almost believe the worst has passed.

Then you see the figures.

They emerge from the far side of the settlement as the last of the violet light disappears. Tall, thin silhouettes move between the ruined buildings, their shapes difficult to distinguish against the smoke. They carry long iron stakes that flash briefly in the moonlight. Their movements are measured and deliberate. They do not hurry. They do not call to one another. They seem to know exactly where they are going.

Even at this distance, something about them makes you hold your breath.

You have heard old stories about the Bone Covens, though you have never given much thought to whether they were true. Tales told in winter, when the fire burned low and children were warned not to wander beyond the boundary stones. Stories of figures who came after disasters, carrying iron and ash, searching the places where ordinary laws had failed.

You watch the figures pass through the ruined village.

They stop beside certain buildings. They drive their stakes into the earth. Occasionally, one of them kneels beside a patch of blackened ground, remaining still for so long that you wonder whether they are listening to something beneath it.

But they never come towards the outer orchards.

They never search the ridge.

Eventually, they disappear into the smoke, leaving the village to the cold light of dawn.

You remain hidden until the last traces of violet have vanished from the sky. Only when the birds begin to call from the trees do you look down at your hands.

Ash coats your fingers. It has settled into the creases of your palms and beneath your nails. You rub at it, but the grey residue seems to cling stubbornly to your skin.

Then you feel it.

A faint vibration beneath the surface of your hands, so subtle that you might mistake it for the lingering tremor of fear. You press your palms together. The sensation remains: a quiet, persistent hum running through your blood.

You have no explanation for it.

You never saw the creature that may have emerged from the ash. You never heard an ancient voice speak your True Name. You never stood in the village square and witnessed the forces that destroyed your home. You chose the trees, the darkness, and the possibility of surviving another day.

You saved what you could.

But whatever happened in the village has not left you untouched.

As dawn spreads over the ruined settlement, you begin to understand that survival is not the same as escape. The world beyond the ridge is already changing, whether you witness it or not. The Bone Covens have begun their work. Something has been disturbed beneath the ashes. And somewhere, beyond your sight, there are locks that remain closed and powers that have not yet awakened.

The strange hum in your blood continues, faint but unmistakable.

Like a key waiting for a lock.

You pull your cloak tighter and turn away from the ruins. There will be questions to answer, shelter to find, and difficult choices ahead. For now, you have only the cold earth beneath you, the people you have kept safe, and the uncertain promise of another morning.

The long, quiet survival begins here.

The long, quiet survival begins beneath the cold canopy of the boundary trees, as the first pale light of dawn bleeds across the eastern ridge.

You have not slept. Every time you closed your eyes, you saw violet fire crawling across familiar rooftops, heard the crack of collapsing beams, and imagined the screams of those you could not reach. Now, with morning creeping into the sky, there is only the wind moving through the pines and the distant groan of timber settling in the ruins below.

Highspire village is gone.

From your shelter among the trees, you can see the remains of your former home scattered across the valley floor. Grey ash blankets the village green. The cottages have collapsed into blackened skeletons, their chimneys standing like broken fingers against the paling sky. Here and there, thin strands of smoke rise from the wreckage, twisting upwards before dissolving into the morning mist.

The unnatural violet fires have guttered out. Nothing remains of their terrible light, only scorched earth and the distant, ghostly silhouettes of the Bone Coven's iron stakes. They stand in uneven rows throughout the ruins, driven deep into the ground as though someone has attempted to pin the village itself to the earth.

You do not know what they were meant to contain.

You do not know what escaped.

You know only that you did not go to the square.

You never faced the thing that emerged beneath the village. You never heard ancient voices speaking a name that belonged to you. You never saw the truth hidden beneath the ordinary lives of Highspire.

Perhaps that ignorance has saved you.

Perhaps it has merely postponed something you cannot yet understand.

You rub your hands together, trying to restore some warmth to your fingers. The soot has worked into the creases of your skin, stubborn despite your attempts to wipe it away. Beneath it, something strange stirs.

A faint vibration runs through your hands and up your arms. It is not pain, nor quite a sensation you can name. It resembles the distant hum of a plucked string, so low that you feel it more than hear it. When you hold your breath, it seems to grow stronger.

Then it fades.

You stare at your fingers.

Nothing appears different. Your skin is unmarked, your hands as ordinary as they were yesterday. Yet somewhere beneath the valley, something answers that faint pulse. You feel it in the earth beneath your boots, in the roots winding between the stones, in the strange, persistent rhythm that seems to have settled inside your blood.

You have no explanation for it.

For now, you decide not to look for one.

Your parents sit close beside you on the damp earth, wrapped in their shared cloaks. Your father's hands tremble as he tries to fasten the clasp at his throat, while your mother leans against his shoulder, her eyes closed. Their breathing is heavy with exhaustion, but steady.

Alive.

You keep looking at them as though the sight might change if you stop paying attention. Your mother opens her eyes eventually and reaches for your hand. She does not ask what happened in the village square, or why the fires burned with such unnatural light. The ruins below provide enough of an answer, and the fear in your expression tells her that there are questions you cannot answer.

She squeezes your fingers.

For the moment, that is all either of you needs.

Isleen sleeps against your shoulder, her face half-hidden beneath your cloak. Even in sleep, she clutches the makeshift bundle of belongings you managed to drag from the collapsing cottage. A few clothes, a little food, and one or two objects that seemed worth saving when the roof began to fall.

You cannot remember choosing what to take. You remember only grabbing whatever your hands found and pulling Isleen towards the back door.

Now her breathing is slow and warm against your arm. You shift carefully, easing the weight of her head against your shoulder, and draw your cloak more closely around her.

She has survived the night. You hold on to that fact as though it were a promise.

You sit alone beneath the sheltering pine boughs, listening to the morning wind whisper through the needles. The damp earth chills you through your clothes, and your stomach aches with hunger, but neither discomfort seems important beside the smoking ruins below.

There is no one beside you to ask what happened or to share the burden of remembering.

When you look towards the valley, you see only the remains of the life you knew: familiar lanes buried beneath ash, the broken outline of the meeting house, and the place where your cottage once stood.

You press your hands together and listen to the silence.

You are alive. For this morning, that must be enough.

You saved what mattered most from the wreckage.

The thought should bring comfort, but it carries its own weight. You survived by turning away, by choosing the people beside you—or yourself—over the desperate cries and terrible light behind you. You cannot know how many others escaped. You cannot know whether anyone else will come searching through the ruins.

You may never learn what happened to Highspire's remaining inhabitants.

Eventually, the sun rises high enough to touch the eastern ridge. The light reveals the narrow track winding between the boundary trees, leading away from the valley towards the outer hills. Beyond them lie scattered farms, abandoned watchposts, and settlements that may not yet have heard what happened here.

There might be shelter along that road. Food. People willing to help.

There might also be soldiers, frightened villagers, or others who would look at the strange signs left by the destruction and decide that you are somehow responsible.

You have no way of knowing.

You gather your belongings and prepare to leave. The road ahead will be difficult, and you cannot carry the whole of your former life with you. But there is still a world beyond these trees, and somewhere within it, you may find a place where you can begin again.

As you turn away from Highspire, the faint vibration returns beneath your skin.

You pause, listening.

Nothing answers from the forest. Nothing moves among the trees.

You continue walking.

The long, quiet survival begins.

choices.text: Begin the journey away from the ruins and seek shelter in the outer hills
Choose to leave your village and everything you know behind you.

text.content:
You run towards the screams.

The smoke claws at your throat as you force your way out of the narrow lane, stumbling over broken slate and fragments of timber. Heat presses against your face, though the night air is bitterly cold. The strange vibration that haunted your cottage has become a deafening hum, rising through the soles of your feet and shaking the stones beneath you.

You pass the baker's house. One wall has collapsed into the street, spilling roof tiles and broken furniture across the cobbles. A cart lies overturned beside the well, its wheels turning slowly despite the absence of any wind. The shutters of the meeting house hang crooked from their hinges. Somewhere nearby, a horse screams in terror.

Then the lane opens onto the village square.

You stop.

The square is an inferno.

Violet fire pours across the cobbles, climbing the walls of buildings without consuming them in any way you recognise. It coils around the village well and rises in tall, twisting columns, casting unnatural shadows across the surrounding houses. The flames pulse rather than flicker, expanding and contracting with the rhythm of a vast, unseen heartbeat.

The light is almost beautiful.

That is what frightens you most.

There is no ordinary orange glow, no familiar crackle of burning wood. The fire makes a thin, glass-like sound, as though thousands of fragile vessels are breaking at once. The air reeks of ozone, old copper, and something darker: the dry, bitter smell of charred bone.

You pull your sleeve across your mouth and take a cautious step forward.

The heat strikes you immediately, but it does not behave as heat should. One moment, your face burns as though you have opened a furnace door; the next, a freezing gust sweeps across your skin. Your breath clouds in front of you even as the flames roar nearby. The cobbles beneath your feet tremble, and thin lines of violet light race between them before disappearing into the cracks.

Around the square, destruction spreads in patterns too precise to be accidental.

The nearest buildings have been struck first, their walls fractured by lines radiating from a single point. Beyond them, the damage forms wider circles, each ring following the contours of the village with impossible regularity. Fences have fallen along curved boundaries. Trees stand blackened on one side and untouched on the other. Even the smoke seems to follow these invisible lines, gathering into spirals above the square.

This is not a fire spreading through a settlement.

Something has erupted from beneath it.

You search the devastation for a familiar face, for anyone who might explain what has happened. You see figures moving through the smoke, some stumbling towards the outer lanes, others crouched beside the injured. A woman drags a child away from a burning doorway. An old man kneels beside the well, his hands pressed over his ears as the hum grows louder.

You want to help them.

But something at the centre of the square catches your attention, and the sight makes the rest of the world seem suddenly distant.

The epicentre.

You know this place.

You know what stood here before the night broke apart. You know the ordinary work you did, the familiar faces you saw, the small decisions that seemed insignificant when you made them.

And now, through the violet fire, you can see how those decisions fit together.

The destruction converges on the cottage where you treated Elsie.

You recognise the doorway before you recognise the house itself. Its wooden frame has split down the middle, and the stones around the threshold have been forced upwards from beneath, leaving a ragged hollow in the earth. Violet light pulses through the gaps between the foundations. The door hangs from one hinge, its surface blistered and blackened, yet the walls remain strangely intact.

You remember Elsie lying beneath her blankets earlier that day. The fever burning in her cheeks. The shallow rhythm of her breathing. The way her small fingers curled around yours while you prepared the herbs you had used countless times before.

You had believed the mixture was helping her.

You had watched the fever ease and felt the familiar relief of a problem solved. Even when the hearth burned with that impossible white light, you had tried to explain it away. You had thought the child was recovering, that the strange occurrences were separate incidents, that the world remained as dependable as it had always been.

Now you understand that something else happened beneath your hands.

The herbs did not merely ease Elsie's fever. Their mixture reacted with something dormant in her blood, a hidden lock that had remained sealed for generations. Your treatment disturbed it. The seal broke, and whatever it had contained answered the breach.

The earth beneath the cottage split open.

A pulse of violet light rises from the hollow, and the stones around the threshold shudder. For one instant, you see thin markings beneath the soil, arranged in a circle around the foundations. They resemble veins in pale stone, converging on a dark point below the house.

Then the markings vanish beneath a wave of smoke.

Your hands begin to shake.

You did not know what lay inside the child you were trying to save. You did not know that an ordinary remedy could become the final pressure against an ancient seal. You were doing what you had always done: tending to the sick, trusting that care and knowledge were enough.

And somehow, without knowing it, you helped break the world open.

The epicentre is your workshop.

You recognise the roof beams first, or what remains of them. The front wall has collapsed into the lane, exposing the workbench, the shelves, and the familiar arrangement of tools that you left in place at the end of the day. Your hammer lies half-buried beneath broken masonry. Tongs and iron scraps are scattered across the floor.

At the centre of the wreckage rests the anvil.

It has split down the middle.

You stare at it, unable to reconcile what you see with the weight of the object you have worked beside for years. The iron surface has separated along a perfectly straight line, exposing a hollow chamber within. Its inner walls are lined with pale, curved fragments resembling bone. Thin grooves run between them, forming a pattern that seems to shift whenever the violet light pulses.

You remember the work you did earlier that day.

The metal had been stubborn, resisting the hammer in ways you could not explain. The strange hum had travelled through the tools and into your hands. When you quenched the iron, the water had hissed more fiercely than expected. You had seen the brief white glow and dismissed it as an effect of the heat.

You thought you were repairing an ordinary piece of metal.

Now you can see the markings that had been hidden beneath its surface. An ancient rune has been ground almost flat, its remaining lines broken where your tools struck the iron. The anvil was not simply a tool. It was a ward-anchor, a piece of a much older mechanism designed to keep something buried.

By heating and reshaping the metal, you weakened the rune. Your blood-warmth, carried through your hands and into the iron, completed what ordinary force had begun. The anchor failed, and the seal it maintained collapsed.

A deep note sounds from somewhere beneath the workshop.

You feel it in your chest before you hear it. The split anvil vibrates against the stones, and a thin stream of violet light spills from its hollow centre.

You step backwards.

Your hands, the hands that have shaped metal, repaired hinges, and made useful things for ordinary people, have touched something they were never meant to disturb.

You did not intend to break anything ancient.

You were simply doing your work.

And now the village is burning around you.

The destruction begins at the forest edge.

You see it beyond the last row of cottages, where the fields give way to the dark trees. The boundary stones that have marked the edge of the village for as long as anyone remembers are scattered across the ground. One lies on its side, half-buried in churned earth. Another has split into several pieces, its moss-covered surface glowing faintly beneath the violet light.

You recognise the stone.

Earlier that day, you moved it to clear a snare.

It had seemed an ordinary nuisance, an obstacle in the place where you needed to work. You remember bracing your shoulder against the mossy surface and shifting it just far enough to free the trapped animal. You remember the scrape of stone against earth, the smell of wet leaves, and the blood that spilled across the disturbed ground.

You thought nothing of it.

Hunters spill blood. Stones are moved. The forest is full of old markers whose original purposes have been forgotten. You had no reason to believe that a small act of practical necessity could have consequences beyond the clearing.

Now the earth around the boundary stone has torn open.

A narrow seam cuts through the ground, running between the roots of the trees and towards the village. Violet light shines from within it, illuminating layers of soil that should never have seen daylight. The air above the opening ripples like heat over a forge, though the night is cold enough to numb your fingers.

You remember the old stories about the cairns in the northern woods. The warnings not to disturb certain stones, not to spill blood upon marked ground, not to dismantle what had been built before the village existed. You had always assumed the tales were meant to discourage children from wandering too far or to give meaning to landmarks no one understood.

But the stone was not a boundary marker.

It was the keystone of an ancient cairn, part of a perimeter built to keep the mortal world separate from the old prisons beyond it. When you moved it, you disturbed the structure. When animal blood soaked into the exposed markings, the remaining seal failed.

The seam widens.

For a heartbeat, you glimpse something beyond it: a darkness that does not resemble the space between trees or the hollow beneath the earth. It seems impossibly deep, filled with distant pinpricks of light that move as though they are watching from the other side.

Then the ground shudders, and the opening disappears beneath a cloud of ash.

You stagger away from the stone.

You have spent your life reading tracks, watching animals, and learning the difference between danger and harmless noise. You know how to recognise a broken branch, a fresh footprint, or the sudden silence that warns of a predator nearby.

But you have never seen a trail that leads out of the world itself.

You moved a stone to clear a snare. You spilled blood where the earth had been disturbed. You did what any hunter might have done.

And somehow, you helped tear open the boundary between the living world and something that should have remained imprisoned.

The realisation strikes with the force of a physical blow.

Your ordinary hands, doing your ordinary work, broke the world open.

The thought is almost impossible to bear. You want to reject it, to find another explanation, to insist that no one could have known what would happen. You did not set out to release anything. You did not summon the violet fire or call whatever lies beneath the earth. You were living your life, as everyone in this village was entitled to do.

But the evidence burns before you.

The light intensifies at the epicentre. The hum deepens until the stones tremble beneath your feet. Somewhere within the smoke, something moves.

You cannot yet see what has emerged.

You know only that the destruction is not finished, and that whatever comes next may have noticed you.

What do you do?

choices.text: Approach the glowing epicentre directly to investigate what broke beneath it.
Search the smoking perimeter first to ensure no villagers are trapped.
Draw back into the shadows of the burning lane to observe.

2.3 The Unbound & The Standoff.title: 2.3 The Unbound & The Standoff
2.3 The Unbound & The Standoff.text:
The smoke tears apart.

Violet flames bend away from the centre of the square as though an invisible hand has seized them, exposing a tall figure standing amid the shattered cobblestones. For a heartbeat, you mistake him for a man. Then he lifts his head, and something in the shape of his face makes that assumption impossible.

He is devastatingly scarred. Pale lines cross his cheekbones and disappear beneath a collar of charred black clothing. Other wounds are deeper, jagged marks that glimmer faintly beneath skin caked with ash. His dark hair hangs in tangled strands around his face, and his eyes burn like banked coals, red-gold light shifting beneath their depths.

At each wrist sits a shattered silver binding ring.

The metal has bitten into his skin. Fragments hang loose, etched with symbols that seem to crawl when you try to focus on them. A thin stream of silver light trickles from the wounds beneath the rings, vanishing before it reaches his hands.

He looks neither at the burning houses nor at the villagers stumbling through the smoke. Their cries do not appear to reach him. He seems unaware of the destruction around him, as though he has emerged from a prison so ancient that the world beyond it has become little more than an inconvenience.

Then his gaze finds you.

Everything else falls away.

The screaming, the crackle of fire, the frantic pounding of feet against stone—all of it recedes beneath the sudden awareness of being seen. His expression changes almost imperceptibly. His shoulders straighten. His fingers curl, and the silver fragments around his wrists tremble.

Recognition passes across his face.

Not surprise. Not confusion.

Recognition.

He takes one step towards you.

“Annan.”

He does not shout. He barely raises his voice above the roar of the flames.

Yet the word strikes you with the force of a physical blow.

Your True Name.

You have never spoken it aloud. You have never heard another person utter it. Until this moment, you have not even known that such a name existed. And yet, as it passes his lips, something deep inside you recognises it—not as a word you have learned, but as a truth you have always carried without understanding.

Your blood catches fire.

Heat surges beneath your skin, racing from your chest to your fingertips. Your knees threaten to buckle. The cobblestones shiver beneath your feet, and for one terrifying instant, you feel the world from somewhere beneath its surface: buried foundations, forgotten chambers, ancient locks turning in their sleep.

The silver rings around his wrists flare in answer.

The Fae closes his eyes briefly, as though the response has confirmed something he desperately needed to know.

“After all this time,” he whispers.

You try to speak, but your throat has tightened. Questions crowd your mind. Who is he? How does he know your name? What is happening to you?

Before you can ask any of them, iron slams into stone.

The first stake strikes the cobblestones to your left, sending sparks across the ground. A second lands behind you, then a third. Heavy iron stakes descend around the square in rapid succession, forming a jagged perimeter that cuts through the smoke and fire.

Figures drop from the burning rooftops.

They land with practised precision, wrapped in dark wool and armour decorated with carved bone charms. Their ward-staves are thick ironwood, banded with black metal and etched with pale markings. As they raise them together, the air tightens. A deep vibration rises from the ground, and black iron bars begin to emerge between the stakes, forming a cage around the square.

The Bone Coven has arrived.

You have heard their name spoken in frightened whispers, usually followed by a warning to keep your doors barred and your questions to yourself. The Coven's Wardens do not hunt ordinary criminals. They pursue forbidden magic, unlicensed bloodlines, and things that should have remained buried.

You had imagined them as distant figures in old stories.

Now they are closing around you.

A man walks through their ranks without haste.

His dark coat is immaculate despite the ash drifting through the square. His silver sigil rings catch the firelight as he adjusts the heavy leather ledger hanging at his hip. There is nothing hurried about his movements, nothing visibly threatened by the burning village or the scarred Fae standing in the centre of the cage.

His grey eyes settle on you.

They contain no panic, no uncertainty, not even the smallest flicker of surprise. He regards you with the cold, absolute certainty of an inquisitor who has finally located a missing manuscript.

“Marek Thorne,” someone whispers nearby. “The First Scholar of Ash and Bone.”

Marek stops several paces away. His gaze briefly examines the Fae's broken bindings before returning to you.

“Step away from the entity we call Balor,” he says.

His voice carries smoothly through the roar of the flames. He sounds like a man addressing a difficult but manageable situation, rather than someone standing in the middle of a village consumed by supernatural fire.

“Your bloodline is an unsealed key, and you are coming into Coven custody.”

“Custody?” you manage.

“Protection, if you prefer a gentler word.” Marek opens his ledger with one gloved hand. “Though I suspect you will find the distinction less important once you understand what your presence has awakened.”

Balor laughs, a short, bitter sound.

“Still dressing chains in scholarly language, Thorne?”

For the first time, Marek's composure shifts. His fingers tighten around the edge of the ledger.

“You have no authority here, Fae.”

“I have been imprisoned for longer than your order has existed.”

“And with good reason.”

Silver light spills more brightly from Balor's wounded wrists. He bares his teeth, and for an instant the air around him seems to buckle. The iron bars shudder. Several Wardens brace their staves against the cobblestones, their bone charms rattling in sudden agitation.

Balor turns towards you.

Up close, you can see the exhaustion beneath his fury. His scars are not merely injuries; they seem to have been carved into him deliberately, each one part of a punishment that has endured long beyond any natural lifetime. Yet the power within him remains immense, coiled tightly beneath the broken bindings.

“They will cage you in bone and ash forever, little key,” he says. “They will take your blood, your memories, and every answer you have a right to claim. Walk into the shadows with me, or burn with them.”

Marek closes the ledger.

“Do not mistake his desperation for honesty, Annan. Balor was bound for a reason. If he escapes this perimeter, the consequences will reach far beyond Highspire.”

Both men know your name. Both claim to understand what you are. Neither has offered you the truth without attaching a threat to it.

Around you, the iron cage continues to close. Beyond it, villagers flee through the burning lanes. Somewhere in the distance, a building collapses with a roar that sends sparks spiralling into the night.

You feel the strange heat still pulsing in your blood.

Balor watches you as though your next breath might decide the fate of something older than the village itself. Marek waits with the patience of a man accustomed to having history eventually obey him.

You stand between the unbound Fae and the order that imprisoned him, with no time to discover which one is telling the truth.

You must choose what happens next.
